title: Green projects will not transform African economies. Value chains will
pullQuote: Green projects will not transform African economies. Value chains will.
body:
Africa does not need more isolated green projects. If the continent is to leverage the green transition to achieve its long-awaited industrialization, it must build integrated green value chains (IGVCs).

Across the continent, billions are flowing into utility-scale solar, wind farms, battery minerals, green hydrogen and EV assembly

Yet in many cases, the structure looks familiar. Raw minerals exported. Finished products imported. Minimal domestic integration. Foreign firms dominate local engineering, procurement and construction. Local firms confined to low-value tasks.

This is not green industrialization. It is green extraction in variegated forms.

Isolated green projects deliver megawatts, improve energy access, attract FDI and create temporary construction jobs. But IGVCs develop supplier ecosystems, enable firm upgrading, build technical capabilities, generate domestic value added and create cumulative industrial learning.

Look at it this way. A solar farm that imports everything creates electricity. However, a solar ecosystem that develops local suppliers, logistics firms, service providers, recyclers, and component manufacturers creates industry.

Simply put, one delivers power; the other reshapes economic structure.

IGVCs are one of the missing links in Africa’s green industrialization. Without them, projects remain enclave-like. And enclave models do not transform economies. They create islands of activity in oceans of informality.

Several structural constraints explain and reinforce enclave dynamics on the continent: Weak domestic supplier networks. Fragmented regional markets. Infrastructure gaps. High cost of capital. Policy uncertainty. Procurement systems focused solely on lowest import cost

Private firms respond rationally to risk. In thin ecosystems, therefore, importing as in the Solar case is safer than sourcing locally.

But this creates a self-reinforcing equilibrium: No ecosystem → no local sourcing → no ecosystem.

So what needs to change?

Green industrial policy in Africa must move beyond project approval toward ecosystem construction by:

- Tying procurement to phased local supplier development
- Supporting technological upgrading of domestic firms
- Developing industrial clusters around renewable zones
- Aggregating regional demand to justify component manufacturing
- Aligning skills systems with specific green industries
- Deploying blended finance to de-risk domestic manufacturing

**Bottom line:** Africa's green industrial future lies on the extent to which it leverages green industrial policy to drive and deliver on the strategies listed above, among others.

Green projects are necessary. IGVCs are transformative. The distinction is not semantic. It is structural.
